q: You see a red sign with eight sides at an intersection, but snow covers the word on it. What must you do?
a: Come to a complete stop
b: Slow down and yield to cross traffic
c: Stop only if cross traffic is coming
d: Continue at the posted speed
exp: The octagon shape is used only for the stop sign, so it means a full stop even when the word cannot be read.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2A.05 and Table 2A-1

q: What does a downward pointing triangle with a red border and a white center tell you to do?
a: Stop completely every time, then go
b: Merge into the left lane
c: Slow down and let traffic already in or near the intersection go first
d: Watch for a railroad crossing ahead
exp: That is the yield sign. You slow down, give the right of way, and may keep moving without a full stop if the way is clear.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Sections 2A.05 and 2B.05

q: Which sign shape tells you a railroad crossing is ahead?
a: A yellow diamond
b: A round yellow sign
c: A yellow pennant
d: A white rectangle
exp: The circle is reserved for the railroad advance warning sign, placed before the tracks.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2A.05 and Table 2A-1

q: A yellow pennant shaped sign appears on the left side of the road. What does it mark?
a: A school crossing
b: A lane that ends ahead
c: A sharp curve to the left
d: The start of a no passing zone
exp: The pennant is used only for the No Passing Zone sign, and it stands on the left where you look before passing.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Table 2A-1 and Section 2C.53

q: A five sided sign shaped like a house with a pointed roof warns you about what?
a: A school zone or school crossing
b: A railroad crossing
c: A hospital ahead
d: A steep hill
exp: The pentagon is reserved for school signs.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2A.05 and Table 2A-1

q: What does an orange diamond shaped sign mean?
a: A school zone ahead
b: A general hazard such as a curve
c: Road work or temporary changes ahead
d: Services such as gas and food
exp: Orange is the color for temporary traffic control in work zones. Yellow is used for general warnings.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 6H.01

q: Which color is used on signs that point you to gas, food, lodging and hospitals?
a: Green
b: Blue
c: Brown
d: Orange
exp: Blue guide signs show motorist services.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2A.06 and Table 2A-2

q: A brown sign most likely points you to which place?
a: A rest area with fuel
b: A highway exit
c: A hospital
d: A state park or historic site
exp: Brown signs guide drivers to recreation and cultural interest areas such as parks and historic sites.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2A.06 and Table 2A-2

q: What does a fluorescent pink sign that reads INCIDENT AHEAD tell you?
a: A crash or emergency scene is ahead
b: A school zone starts here
c: A toll plaza is ahead
d: A detour is permanent
exp: Fluorescent pink is used for incident management signs at crash and emergency scenes.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 6H.01

q: Which statement about regulatory signs is correct?
a: They only suggest a safe speed
b: They state a law you must obey
c: They point to services and exits
d: They warn of hazards but carry no legal force
exp: Regulatory signs, such as Stop, Speed Limit and One Way, give rules that can be enforced.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Chapter 2B

q: Most warning signs have what shape and color?
a: A white rectangle with black letters
b: A green rectangle with white letters
c: A yellow diamond with black symbols or words
d: A red circle with a white bar
exp: Warning signs are generally yellow diamonds with a black legend and border.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2C.02

q: Most guide signs on highways, showing exits and distances, are what color?
a: Yellow with black letters
b: Orange with black letters
c: Brown with white letters
d: Green with white letters
exp: Green is the color for direction and destination guide signs.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2A.06 and Table 2A-2

q: You are driving and pass a red rectangle sign with white letters reading WRONG WAY facing you. What does it mean?
a: You are driving against traffic and must safely turn around
b: Traffic ahead is merging from the left
c: The road ahead is closed for repairs
d: You must stop and then continue
exp: A Wrong Way sign faces drivers who have entered a one way road or ramp in the wrong direction.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2B.47

q: Where are you most likely to see a Do Not Enter sign?
a: At the start of a school zone
b: At the exit end of a freeway ramp
c: Before a sharp curve
d: At a rest area entrance
exp: Do Not Enter signs stand where traffic may not go in from that direction, such as freeway exit ramps and the far end of one way streets.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2B.46

q: A yellow plaque reading 25 MPH sits under a curve warning sign. What does it show?
a: The legal speed limit for the whole road
b: The minimum speed allowed in the curve
c: The advised top speed for the curve in good conditions
d: The speed limit for trucks only
exp: This is an advisory speed plaque. It is advice for the curve, while the legal limit is posted on a white Speed Limit sign.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2C.59

q: Which sign shows the maximum legal speed on a road?
a: A yellow square plaque under a warning sign
b: An orange diamond
c: A yellow diamond with a number
d: A white rectangle with black numbers
exp: Speed Limit signs are white regulatory signs. Yellow speed plaques are advisory only.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2B.21

q: What is the difference between a Merge sign and a Lane Ends sign?
a: Merge means traffic is joining your road; Lane Ends means your road is losing a lane
b: They mean the same thing
c: Merge means your lane ends; Lane Ends means traffic joins from a ramp
d: Merge is a rule; Lane Ends is only a suggestion
exp: A Merge sign warns that traffic will enter from another road, while a Lane Ends sign warns that one lane is about to end.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Sections 2C.45 and 2C.47

q: A yellow sign shows two arrows, one pointing up and one pointing down. What does it warn you about?
a: A divided highway begins
b: Two way traffic is ahead
c: You must make a U-turn
d: The road splits into two lanes going your way
exp: The Two Way Traffic sign warns that you are leaving a one way or divided road and oncoming traffic is ahead.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2C.21

q: What does a Divided Highway Ends sign tell you?
a: A median will soon separate the two directions
b: You are entering a one way street
c: Traffic will soon travel in both directions with no median between you
d: The right lane ends ahead
exp: When a divided highway ends, oncoming traffic is no longer separated from you by a divider.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2C.21

q: What does a School Speed Limit sign with a WHEN FLASHING plaque mean?
a: You may drive at any speed while the lights flash
b: The limit applies only on weekends
c: You must stop when the lights flash
d: The lower school limit applies while the yellow lights on the sign are flashing
exp: A WHEN FLASHING plaque means the reduced school limit is in force only while the sign's yellow beacons are flashing.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 7B.05 and Figure 7B-1

q: A school sign has a small plaque below it with an arrow pointing down at an angle. What does it mark?
a: The school crossing itself
b: The end of the school zone
c: A school bus stop two miles ahead
d: A parking area for parents
exp: The school sign with a diagonal downward arrow plaque marks the location of the school crosswalk.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 7B.03

q: A crossing guard in a school zone holds up a STOP paddle. What should you do?
a: Slow down and drive around the children
b: Stop and wait until the guard signals you to go
c: Stop only if a child is in your lane
d: Sound your horn and continue slowly
exp: Crossing guards stand in the road to stop all traffic, and drivers obey them like a stop sign.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 7D.02

q: When does a school zone end?
a: When you can no longer see the school building
b: When you pass the school crossing
c: When you pass the End School Zone sign
d: As soon as no children are in sight
exp: An End School Zone sign marks the downstream end of the zone. Keep the school limit until you pass it.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 7B.02

q: A flagger in a work zone turns the paddle so that SLOW faces you. What should you do?
a: Stop and wait for a police officer
b: Speed up to clear the zone quickly
c: Change lanes immediately
d: Move ahead slowly and watch for workers
exp: The SLOW face means you may proceed with caution through the work area.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 6D.05

q: In a work zone, a flagger's signal and a nearby sign seem to give different directions. Whose directions do you follow?
a: The flagger's
b: The sign's
c: Whichever lets you move faster
d: The car in front of you
exp: A flagger controls traffic as it is right now, so the flagger's directions come first inside the work zone.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 6D.05

q: A large lighted arrow board in a work zone shows an arrow flashing to the left. What should you do?
a: Stay in your lane and speed up
b: Merge left early and smoothly because the lane ahead is closed
c: Turn left at the next street
d: Stop until the arrow turns off
exp: A flashing arrow on an arrow board means a lane is closed ahead and traffic must move in the direction of the arrow.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 6L.06

q: Drums, cones, vertical panels and barricades in a work zone are known as what?
a: Speed control devices that measure your speed
b: Parking markers for work trucks
c: Channeling devices that guide you through the zone
d: Signs that show detour distances
exp: These orange and white devices guide traffic along a safe path and keep drivers out of the work area.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Part 6

q: An Interstate route has an even number, such as 80. Which way does it usually run?
a: It runs mostly north and south
b: It loops around a city
c: It is a toll road
d: It runs mostly east and west
exp: Interstates with even numbers run mostly east and west; odd numbers run mostly north and south.
src: FHWA Interstate System numbering (fhwa.dot.gov/interstate/faq.cfm); MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2D.11

q: What does a yellow sign showing a car with wavy marks behind it mean?
a: The road has sharp curves
b: Loose gravel is falling from trucks
c: The road is slippery when wet
d: The road ahead is under repair
exp: This is the Slippery When Wet sign. Slow down in rain and avoid sudden braking or steering.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2C.30

q: Why do stop, yield and railroad signs have shapes that no other sign may use?
a: Because they are cheaper to make
b: Because only these signs are reflective
c: So they can be placed on the left side of the road
d: So drivers can recognize them from the shape alone, even at night or when the words are covered
exp: Reserved shapes let drivers identify the most important signs from a distance and from behind.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2A.05 and Table 2A-1

q: The posted limit is 45 mph, but heavy rain makes it hard to see the road ahead. What speed does the basic speed law require?
a: Exactly 45 mph
b: A speed that is safe for the rain and the distance you can see
c: Any speed up to 45 mph
d: 45 mph if you turn on your headlights
exp: The basic speed law says you may never drive faster than is safe for current conditions, even when you are under the posted limit.
src: State basic speed law; NHTSA Speeding, https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/speeding

q: What does the number on a white Speed Limit sign tell you?
a: The speed you must drive
b: The lowest speed allowed
c: The suggested speed for curves
d: The highest legal speed in good conditions
exp: A posted limit is a ceiling for good conditions, not a target. Bad conditions call for a lower speed.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2B.21

q: Can you get a ticket for speeding while driving below the posted limit?
a: No, never
b: Only on a freeway
c: Yes, if your speed is too fast for the conditions
d: Only at night
exp: Under the basic speed law, an officer can cite you for driving too fast for weather, traffic or road conditions even below the limit.
src: State basic speed law; NHTSA Speeding, https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/speeding

q: Why can driving far below the speed of other traffic be dangerous?
a: Other drivers bunch up behind you and make risky passes
b: It wears out your brakes
c: It uses more fuel
d: It is never dangerous
exp: A car moving much slower than the flow causes tailgating and unsafe passing. Most states ban driving so slowly that you block normal traffic.
src: State minimum speed laws; California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: Which three parts add up to your total stopping distance?
a: Perception distance, reaction distance and braking distance
b: Following distance, braking distance and skid distance
c: Reaction distance, coasting distance and parking distance
d: Sight distance, passing distance and braking distance
exp: Total stopping distance is the distance traveled while you notice the hazard, while your foot moves to the brake, and while the brakes stop the car.
src: NHTSA and state driver manuals, stopping distance

q: During perception and reaction time, what is your car doing?
a: Still moving at full speed
b: Slowing down quickly
c: Standing still
d: Skidding
exp: The car does not slow until you press the brake, so it keeps going at the same speed while you notice and react.
src: State driver manuals, stopping distance

q: If you double your speed, about how much longer is your braking distance?
a: About the same
b: About twice as long
c: About four times as long
d: About half as long
exp: Braking distance grows with the square of speed, so twice the speed needs about four times the distance to brake.
src: State driver manuals, stopping distance

q: Which of these makes your braking distance longer?
a: A dry road surface
b: A wet road surface
c: Driving uphill
d: Driving slower
exp: Wet, icy or loose surfaces give the tires less grip, so the car needs more distance to stop.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: Which of these makes your perception and reaction distance longer?
a: Driving on a dry road
b: Having new tires
c: Driving uphill
d: Being tired or distracted
exp: Fatigue, distraction, alcohol and drugs slow the time it takes you to notice a hazard and hit the brake.
src: NHTSA Distracted Driving, https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/distracted-driving

q: At night, how fast should you drive in relation to your headlights?
a: At the posted limit, whatever you can see
b: Fast enough to keep up with the car ahead
c: Slow enough to stop within the distance your headlights light up
d: Slow enough to stop within twice your headlight range
exp: You should always be able to stop within the distance you can see clearly. At night that is the reach of your headlights.
src: State driver manuals, night driving and speed

q: What is the best way to measure your following distance?
a: Count car lengths between you and the car ahead
b: Watch your speedometer
c: Count the seconds between the car ahead and you passing a fixed point
d: Wait until the car ahead brakes
exp: Pick a fixed object; when the car ahead passes it, count until you reach it. A time gap grows as your speed grows.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: You are counting your following distance and you reach the fixed point before you finish the count. What should you do?
a: Ease off the gas to open the gap
b: Change lanes right away
c: Flash your headlights
d: Keep the same speed
exp: Reaching the point early means you are too close. Slowing slightly lets the gap grow.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: When should you leave more following distance than normal?
a: When following a large truck that blocks your view
b: When the road is dry and clear
c: When traffic is light
d: When you are driving in daylight
exp: Large vehicles block your view of the road ahead, so you need more room to see and react.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: Why should you leave extra room when following a motorcycle?
a: Motorcycles are always slower than cars
b: Motorcycles cannot use their brakes
c: The law forbids following motorcycles
d: A motorcycle can stop quickly and its rider can fall
exp: Motorcycles can stop in less distance than cars and riders can go down suddenly, so more space gives you time to stop.
src: NHTSA Motorcycle Safety, https://www.nhtsa.gov/road-safety/motorcycles

q: Which situation calls for more following distance?
a: A dry, straight road at noon
b: A quiet street with no parked cars
c: A wet road covered with leaves
d: An empty parking lot
exp: Wet or slippery surfaces increase stopping distance, so add time to your gap.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: A driver is tailgating you. What is the safest thing to do?
a: Slam on your brakes to warn the driver
b: Speed up to get away
c: Stay in the left lane and slow to a crawl
d: Move to the right lane if you can and let the driver pass
exp: Letting a tailgater pass removes the danger behind you. Sudden braking can cause a rear end crash.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: A tailgater is behind you and you cannot change lanes. How should you adjust your space ahead?
a: Close the gap to the car ahead
b: Leave more room in front of you
c: Keep the gap exactly the same
d: Drive on the shoulder
exp: More space ahead lets you slow down gently, so the driver behind you is less likely to hit you.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: What is a space cushion?
a: The padding inside your seat
b: Open room on every side of your car
c: The gap between parked cars
d: The shoulder of a highway
exp: A space cushion is open space ahead, behind and to each side that gives you time and room to react.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: Parked cars are on your right and oncoming traffic is on your left, both equally close. Where should you steer?
a: Close to the parked cars
b: A middle path between the two
c: Close to the center line
d: Onto the shoulder
exp: When hazards on both sides are equal, steer between them to keep some space from each.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: On a road with several lanes, why should you avoid driving right beside another car for a long time?
a: You stay in its blind spot and lose your escape path
b: It is always illegal
c: It wastes fuel
d: It makes your mirrors fog up
exp: Riding beside another car puts you in each other's blind spots and blocks a side escape. Move ahead or drop back.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: Why should you leave room between your car and parked cars?
a: Parked cars may start to roll
b: It helps you parallel park
c: A door may open or a car may pull out
d: It keeps your tires clean
exp: Doors opening and cars pulling out are common hazards along a row of parked cars.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: About how far ahead should you look when you drive?
a: Only at the bumper of the car in front
b: About 2 seconds ahead
c: As far as the next exit, ignoring the near road
d: About 10 to 15 seconds ahead
exp: Looking 10 to 15 seconds ahead, about a block in the city or a quarter mile on the highway, lets you find problems early.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: At an intersection, why do you look left a second time before you go?
a: Traffic from the right is always faster
b: The law requires two looks to the right
c: It helps you see the signal
d: Traffic from the left reaches your path first
exp: Cars approaching from the left are in the near lane and reach you first, so check that side last.
src: State driver manuals, scanning at intersections

q: How often should you check your mirrors while driving?
a: Only when you change lanes
b: Once at the start of each trip
c: Every few seconds, and before you slow, turn or change lanes
d: Only when a car honks
exp: Frequent mirror checks keep you aware of traffic around you, especially before any change in speed or position.
src: State driver manuals, scanning

q: What is a blind spot?
a: A dark stretch of road
b: A spot where parking is banned
c: A crack in the windshield
d: An area around your car you cannot see in your mirrors
exp: Blind spots are areas, mainly behind each shoulder, that your mirrors do not show.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: How should you check your blind spot before changing lanes?
a: Check your inside mirror only
b: Turn your head and look over your shoulder
c: Rely on your side mirror only
d: Watch for other drivers to honk
exp: Mirrors leave blind spots. A quick look over your shoulder through the side window is the only full check.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: Your car has blind spot warning lights. What does that mean for your lane changes?
a: You no longer need to check at all
b: You still need to turn your head and look
c: You can change lanes without signaling
d: You only need to check your inside mirror
exp: Sensors can miss vehicles and can be blocked by dirt or snow. They help but do not replace a head check.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: How should you set your side mirrors to reduce blind spots?
a: So you can barely see the side of your own car
b: So you see mostly the side of your own car
c: Pointed at the ground
d: Pointed at the sky
exp: Turning the mirrors outward until your car just shows at the inner edge shows more of the next lane.
src: State driver manuals, mirror adjustment

q: When you pass another car on a multi-lane road, how should you move through its blind spot?
a: Slowly, staying beside it
b: By honking first and waiting
c: By dropping back into it
d: Steadily, without lingering beside it
exp: Spending as little time as you safely can in another driver's blind spot lowers the chance they move into you.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Managing Space, https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dmv/driver-services/pennsylvania-drivers-manual/online-drivers-manual/everyday-driving-skills/managing-space

q: Some freeways post a minimum speed. What should you do in heavy snow if that speed is unsafe?
a: Drive slower, stay in the right lane and leave at a safe exit if needed
b: Drive at the minimum speed no matter what
c: Speed up to the maximum limit
d: Stop in the travel lane
exp: Safety comes first. In bad conditions you may drive below the minimum, keep right and leave the freeway if conditions stay bad.
src: State minimum speed laws; State basic speed law

q: On a road with two lanes going your way, which lane should you use for normal driving?
a: The left lane
b: The right lane
c: Either lane, switching often
d: The shoulder
exp: Most states follow keep right except to pass. The left lane is for passing and left turns.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: What is the left lane of a multi-lane highway mainly for?
a: Slow traffic
b: Entering and leaving the highway
c: Passing and getting ready to turn left
d: Parking in an emergency
exp: The left lane is used to pass or turn left. Slower traffic and entering and exiting traffic use the right lane.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: What is the correct order of steps for a lane change?
a: Signal, move, then check mirrors
b: Move, then signal
c: Head check, move, then signal
d: Mirrors, signal, head check, then move
exp: Check your mirrors, signal, glance over your shoulder at the blind spot, then move smoothly.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: You want to move from the far left lane to an exit on the right, three lanes over. How should you do it?
a: Change one lane at a time, checking and signaling each time
b: Cross all three lanes in one move
c: Slow down sharply and cut across
d: Use the shoulder to get over
exp: Moving one lane at a time lets you check each lane and lets other drivers see what you are doing.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: On a road with three lanes your way, you want to move into the middle lane. What extra check should you make?
a: Look at the far lane, in case a car there moves into the middle too
b: Look at the oncoming traffic
c: Check the speedometer
d: Check your fuel gauge
exp: A driver two lanes over may aim for the same open space at the same moment.
src: State driver manuals, changing lanes

q: What does a double solid white line between two lanes mean?
a: You may cross it freely
b: You may not cross it
c: You may cross it only to pass
d: It marks a bike lane
exp: Double solid white lane lines mark places where crossing is prohibited.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 3B.06

q: On a two-lane road, when may you pass on the left?
a: When the line on your side is broken and the road ahead is clear far enough
b: Whenever the car ahead is slow
c: When a solid yellow line is on your side
d: Near the top of a hill if you hurry
exp: You may pass only with a broken line on your side, no sign forbidding it and enough clear road to finish safely.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: You are passing a car. When is it safe to return to your lane?
a: As soon as your front bumper passes its front bumper
b: When you are side by side with it
c: When the driver waves at you
d: When you can see both of its headlights in your inside mirror
exp: Seeing both headlights of the passed car in your inside mirror means you have room to pull back in.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: The line on your side of the center line is broken, but a hill crest just ahead blocks your view. May you pass?
a: Yes, the broken line allows it
b: Yes, if you speed up a lot
c: No, you cannot see oncoming traffic
d: Yes, if you honk first
exp: Passing is not allowed near a curve or hill crest where you cannot see far enough ahead, whatever the line says.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: Which of these is a place where you may not pass on a two-lane road?
a: At a railroad crossing
b: On a long straight road with a broken line
c: On a clear road in daylight
d: Where a sign says Pass With Care
exp: Passing is banned at or near railroad crossings, intersections, bridges and tunnels.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: While passing, what speed limit applies?
a: You may exceed the limit by 10 mph
b: There is no limit while passing
c: You must go double the other car's speed
d: You may not go over the posted limit
exp: The speed limit applies while you pass. If you cannot pass without speeding, do not pass.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: You started to pass, but an oncoming car appears and you cannot finish in time. What should you do?
a: Speed up as fast as you can
b: Drive onto the left shoulder
c: Slow down, drop back and return to your lane behind the car
d: Stop in the oncoming lane
exp: Giving up on a pass is always safer than forcing it.
src: State driver manuals, passing

q: When may you pass another vehicle on the right?
a: Whenever the right shoulder is open
b: Any time on a two-lane road
c: When the vehicle ahead is turning left
d: When the vehicle ahead is going the speed limit
exp: Passing on the right is allowed when a car ahead is turning left or on roads with two or more lanes your way, never on the shoulder.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: May you drive on the shoulder to pass a car on the right?
a: Yes, if you signal
b: No, unless a sign or an officer allows it
c: Yes, at low speed
d: Yes, on any freeway
exp: Drivers may not use the shoulder or edge of the road to pass unless signs or an officer direct it.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: Another car is passing you on a two-lane road. What should you do?
a: Speed up so it cannot pass
b: Move toward the center line
c: Stay in your lane and keep a steady speed or slow slightly
d: Flash your high beams
exp: Help the passing driver get by. Never speed up while being passed.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: Many cars are passing you on the right on a multi-lane highway. What does that tell you?
a: You should speed up in the left lane
b: You should move to a lane farther right
c: The other drivers are breaking the law
d: You should stop on the shoulder
exp: If traffic keeps passing on your right, you are holding up the left lane. Move right when safe.
src: New York State Driver's Manual, Chapter 6 Passing, https://dmv.ny.gov/new-york-state-drivers-manual-practice-tests/chapter-6-passing

q: A car is passing you at night. What should you do with your headlights?
a: Switch to low beams
b: Switch to high beams
c: Turn them off
d: Flash them twice
exp: Low beams keep you from blinding the passing driver as they pull alongside.
src: State driver manuals, night driving

q: What is the acceleration lane on a freeway entrance for?
a: Reaching the speed of freeway traffic before you merge
b: Stopping to wait for a gap
c: Passing slow cars on the freeway
d: Parking in an emergency
exp: The acceleration lane gives you room to match the speed of traffic so you can merge smoothly.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 3B.07; California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: As you merge onto a freeway, who usually has the right of way?
a: You, because you are merging
b: Whoever is going faster
c: Traffic already on the freeway
d: Trucks only
exp: Drivers on the freeway usually have the right of way. You must find a gap and fit in.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: Why should you avoid stopping at the end of an acceleration lane?
a: It is always against the law to stop anywhere
b: It damages your brakes
c: It confuses traffic signals
d: Joining fast traffic from a stop is very hard and dangerous
exp: From a stop you cannot reach freeway speed in time. Stop only if there is truly no gap.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: You are driving in the right lane of a freeway and see a car on the on-ramp. What should you do?
a: Speed up to block it
b: Stop in your lane
c: Move left a lane if safe, or adjust speed to let it in
d: Honk until it stops
exp: Making room for merging traffic keeps the freeway flowing and prevents crashes.
src: State driver manuals, freeway driving

q: Where should you do most of your slowing when leaving a freeway?
a: In the left lane of the freeway
b: In the travel lane before the exit
c: On the shoulder
d: In the deceleration lane or on the exit ramp
exp: Slowing in the freeway lane can cause a rear end crash. Move into the deceleration lane, then slow.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 3B.07; California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: You just missed your freeway exit. What should you do?
a: Back up on the shoulder
b: Go on to the next exit
c: Stop and wait for a gap to reverse
d: Cut across the painted area to the ramp
exp: Never back up or turn around on a freeway. Take the next exit and come back.
src: State driver manuals, freeway driving

q: What is highway hypnosis?
a: A type of road sign
b: A medicine side effect
c: A legal speed zone
d: A dull, half awake state from long, monotonous driving
exp: Long straight drives can lull you so you notice less. Keep your eyes moving and take breaks.
src: State driver manuals, freeway driving

q: After a long time at high speed on a freeway, why should you check your speedometer on the exit ramp?
a: The speedometer stops working at high speed
b: Lower speeds can feel slower than they really are
c: Ramps have no speed limits
d: It is required on every road test
exp: After high speed driving, a moderate speed feels like a crawl, so you may take the ramp too fast.
src: State driver manuals, freeway driving

q: What does a white diamond painted in a lane mean?
a: It is a bike lane
b: It is a bus stop
c: It marks a railroad crossing
d: It is a high occupancy vehicle (HOV) lane
exp: The diamond symbol is used only for HOV preferential lanes.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Chapter 2G, Sections 2G.03 and 2G.10; California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: A sign over a lane reads HOV 2+. Who may use the lane while the rule is in effect?
a: Vehicles carrying at least two people, counting the driver
b: Only vehicles with two or more drivers
c: Only vehicles with two axles
d: Any vehicle going over the limit
exp: The number after HOV is the minimum number of people in the vehicle, including the driver.
src: MUTCD 11th ed., Section 2G.05

q: An HOV lane is separated from the other lanes by a double solid white line. Where may you enter it?
a: Anywhere you like
b: Anywhere, if you signal
c: Only from the shoulder
d: Only where the lines are broken or signs show an opening
exp: Crossing double solid lines into or out of a special lane is not allowed. Use the marked openings.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: Your car starts to fail on a freeway. What should you do first?
a: Stop right away in your lane
b: Turn on your hazard lights and steer onto the right shoulder
c: Turn off the engine at speed
d: Get out and push the car
exp: Flashers warn others, and getting as far off the road as you can keeps you out of traffic.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: Your car has broken down on the shoulder of a busy highway and it is not on fire. In most cases, what is safest?
a: Stay in the car with your seat belt on and call for help
b: Stand behind the car to wave at traffic
c: Walk along the travel lane to find help
d: Sit on the guardrail beside the car
exp: People standing by a disabled car are at great risk. Stay buckled in unless the car is unsafe or a safe spot away from traffic is close.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads, https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads/

q: You park facing downhill next to a curb. Which way should you turn your front wheels?
a: Away from the curb
b: Toward the curb
c: Straight ahead
d: It does not matter
exp: Wheels turned toward the curb make the car roll into the curb if it moves.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: You park facing uphill next to a curb. Which way should you turn your front wheels?
a: Toward the curb
b: Straight ahead
c: Toward the curb, then straight
d: Away from the curb
exp: Turned away from the curb, the car rolls back and the front tire stops against the curb.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: You park on a hill on a road with no curb. Which way should you turn your front wheels?
a: Toward the edge of the road
b: Toward the center of the road
c: Straight ahead
d: Away from the shoulder
exp: With no curb, turning the wheels toward the side means the car rolls off the road, not into traffic.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: Which steps should you take every time you park on a hill?
a: Leave the car in neutral
b: Leave the engine running
c: Shift to park, set the parking brake and turn the wheels correctly
d: Turn the wheels straight and leave the brake off
exp: On a hill the parking brake and the wheel position work together to keep the car from rolling into traffic.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: Uphill with a curb, after turning the wheels, what do you do next?
a: Let the car roll back slowly until the front tire rests on the curb
b: Pull forward onto the curb
c: Turn the wheels straight again
d: Leave a gap of several feet from the curb
exp: Letting the tire settle against the curb lets the curb hold the car.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What does a red painted curb usually mean?
a: Loading zone only
b: Parking for a limited time
c: No stopping, standing or parking
d: Parking for people with disabilities
exp: Where curb colors are used, red means you may not stop, stand or park.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What does a blue painted curb usually mean?
a: Parking only for people with a disability placard or plate
b: Short time parking
c: Loading zone
d: No parking at any time
exp: Blue marks spaces reserved for drivers with disabilities or drivers carrying them, with a valid placard or plate.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What does a green painted curb usually mean?
a: No stopping
b: Parking for a limited time
c: Fire lane
d: Bus stop only
exp: Green allows parking for a limited time, shown on a sign or painted on the curb.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What does a white painted curb usually mean?
a: Park all day
b: No stopping at any time
c: Disability parking
d: Stop only long enough to pick up or drop off people
exp: White allows a short stop to load or unload passengers or mail.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What does a yellow painted curb usually mean?
a: Parking for people with disabilities
b: Park as long as you like
c: Loading zone; stop only to load or unload
d: Bike parking only
exp: Yellow marks a loading zone with a time limit.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: Which of these is a place where you may never park?
a: In a marked space in a lot
b: Along a curb with no signs or paint
c: In a crosswalk
d: In your own driveway
exp: Parking in a crosswalk blocks people walking and hides them from drivers. It is banned in every state.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What does double parking mean?
a: Parking on the street side of a car already parked at the curb
b: Parking across two spaces in a lot
c: Parking with two wheels on the curb
d: Parking in the same space twice a day
exp: A double parked car blocks a traffic lane and is not allowed.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: Which of these places is off limits for parking in every state?
a: Beside a green curb
b: In a marked parallel space
c: In a parking garage
d: Next to a fire hydrant
exp: A car beside a hydrant blocks firefighters. The exact distance comes from state law.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: May you park in the striped area next to a disability parking space?
a: Yes, if you have a small car
b: Yes, for up to 15 minutes
c: No, that area is needed for wheelchairs and ramps
d: Yes, at night
exp: The striped access aisle must stay clear so a person can get in and out of a vehicle.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: A sign reads No Stopping. What may you do there?
a: Stop only to obey a signal or officer, or to avoid a crash
b: Stop briefly to drop off a friend
c: Stop to load packages
d: Park for up to 10 minutes
exp: No Stopping is the strictest of these signs. You may not stop at all except to obey traffic control or avoid a crash.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: Which sign still allows you to stop briefly to load or unload things?
a: No Stopping
b: No Parking
c: No Standing
d: Do Not Enter
exp: No Parking forbids leaving the car, but a brief stop to load or unload is allowed.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: In parallel parking, where should you stop before you start backing?
a: Behind the space, in the lane
b: Halfway into the space
c: Beside the car behind the space
d: Beside the car ahead of the space, with your rear bumpers even
exp: Starting even with the car ahead, about two to three feet out, gives you the right angle to back in.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: While backing into a parallel space, at about what angle should your car be before you straighten the wheel?
a: About 10 degrees
b: About 45 degrees
c: About 90 degrees
d: Straight in line with the curb
exp: Back to about a 45 degree angle, then straighten, then turn the other way to swing in.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: How long should a parallel parking space be?
a: Several feet longer than your car
b: Exactly the length of your car
c: Shorter than your car
d: Twice the width of your car
exp: You need extra room in front and behind to swing the car into the space.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: Your first parallel parking try goes badly. What is the best choice?
a: Push the car into the curb
b: Leave it far from the curb
c: Pull out and start again
d: Use the bumpers of the other cars to guide you
exp: A clean second try is better than many small corrections or hitting the curb.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: Before you open your door after parking on a street, what should you do?
a: Open it quickly to save time
b: Check mirrors and look over your shoulder for traffic and bikes
c: Honk to warn others
d: Turn on your high beams
exp: A door opened into traffic can hit a cyclist or be struck by a passing car.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: What should you do before you leave your parked car?
a: Leave the engine running
b: Leave a child in the car for a minute
c: Shift to neutral
d: Set the parking brake and take the key with you
exp: Setting the brake and taking the key keeps the car from rolling or being driven off.
src: California Driver Handbook, Navigating the Roads (cont.), https://dmv.ca.gov/portal/handbook/california-driver-handbook/navigating-the-roads-cont1/

q: How should you look when you back straight up?
a: Use only your inside mirror
b: Use only your side mirrors
c: Look straight ahead
d: Turn your body and look back through the rear window
exp: Turning to look back gives you the widest view. Mirrors alone leave large areas you cannot see.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: You want the back of your car to go right while backing. Which way do you turn the wheel?
a: To the left
b: Keep it straight
c: To the right
d: Turn it all the way left, then right
exp: When backing, turn the wheel in the direction you want the rear of the car to go.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: How fast should you back up?
a: At the posted speed limit
b: Quickly, to spend less time in reverse
c: At the same speed you drive forward
d: Slowly, at about walking speed or less
exp: Low speed gives you time to stop for anything you did not see behind the car.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: Your car has a backup camera. How should you use it?
a: As your only check
b: As a helper, along with mirrors and looking over your shoulder
c: Only at night
d: Only on the road test
exp: Cameras do not show everything and can be blocked. Look back yourself as well.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: You are backing out of a driveway onto a street. Where should you stop first to look?
a: At the sidewalk, to check for people walking
b: In the middle of the street
c: Only at the far curb
d: You should not stop at all
exp: Stopping at the sidewalk lets you check for people before you look for street traffic.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: You are pulling away from the curb into traffic. What should you do?
a: Pull out quickly and let others slow down
b: Signal, look over your shoulder, and wait for a safe gap
c: Honk and pull out
d: Pull out without signaling
exp: Drivers already on the road have the right of way, so you must wait for a gap after checking your blind spot.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: Why should you look over your shoulder before pulling out from a parallel space?
a: To see if the meter has expired
b: To check your rear tire
c: To read signs behind you
d: A car or bike may be hidden in your blind spot
exp: Your mirrors do not show the blind spot beside and behind you, where a car or cyclist may be coming.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: You are driving out of an alley onto a street. What should you do before crossing the sidewalk?
a: Stop and yield to people walking
b: Honk and keep going
c: Speed up to clear the sidewalk
d: Flash your lights and enter
exp: Most states require a stop before the sidewalk when leaving an alley or driveway, then you yield to traffic.
src: State driver manuals, parking and backing

q: Which driving ability does alcohol affect first, often before the drinker feels drunk?
a: Judgment
b: Hearing
c: Muscle strength
d: Memory of traffic laws
exp: Alcohol dulls judgment first, which is why people who have been drinking often decide they are fine to drive.
src: NHTSA, Drunk Driving (effects of BAC); state driver manuals, alcohol section

q: You have had three beers at a party and need to drive in 30 minutes. What will lower your blood alcohol concentration?
a: Drinking two cups of black coffee
b: Only time
c: Taking a cold shower
d: Eating a large meal now
exp: Your liver clears alcohol at a slow, steady rate. Coffee, showers and food after drinking do not lower BAC.
src: NIAAA; state driver manuals, alcohol section

q: What does BAC stand for?
a: Breath alcohol count
b: Basic alcohol check
c: Blood alcohol concentration
d: Blood absorption control
exp: BAC is the share of alcohol in your blood, measured by a breath, blood or urine test.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/drunk-driving

q: For drivers 21 and older, what BAC is illegal in every state except Utah?
a: 0.10 or higher
b: 0.12 or higher
c: 0.15 or higher
d: 0.08 or higher
exp: All states except Utah set the adult limit at 0.08. Utah's limit is 0.05.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/drunk-driving

q: Which state has a lower adult BAC limit than the 0.08 used everywhere else?
a: Texas
b: Utah
c: Florida
d: New York
exp: Utah lowered its adult limit to 0.05; every other state uses 0.08.
src: https://highwaysafety.utah.gov/05-bac-law/

q: Which of these drinks holds about the same amount of alcohol as 12 ounces of regular beer?
a: A 12 ounce glass of wine
b: Two 1.5 ounce shots of liquor
c: A 1.5 ounce shot of 80 proof liquor
d: A 24 ounce can of malt liquor
exp: A standard drink is 12 ounces of beer, 5 ounces of wine or 1.5 ounces of 80 proof liquor. Each holds about the same alcohol.
src: https://www.niaaa.nih.gov/alcohols-effects-health/what-standard-drink

q: Two friends each drink the same amount in the same hour. Which one is likely to reach the higher BAC?
a: The one who drank beer instead of liquor
b: The one who drank more water afterward
c: The one who is taller but weighs the same
d: The one who weighs less
exp: Body size matters: a smaller person reaches a higher BAC from the same amount of alcohol.
src: State driver manuals, factors affecting BAC

q: Can you be arrested for impaired driving with a BAC below the legal limit?
a: Yes, if alcohol has affected your driving
b: No, never
c: Only if you are over 21
d: Only if you are driving a truck
exp: The limit is not a safe level. Officers can charge you when alcohol has impaired your driving, even below 0.08.
src: State driver manuals, impaired driving section

q: What is a zero tolerance law?
a: A ban on alcohol in every car
b: A rule that all drivers must take a breath test
c: A very low BAC limit for drivers under 21
d: A law that sets the adult limit at zero
exp: Every state has a zero tolerance law that sets a far lower BAC limit for drivers under 21, low enough that one drink can break it.
src: 23 U.S.C. 161 (zero tolerance requirement); state driver manuals

q: What does implied consent mean?
a: You may refuse any test without penalty
b: Police need your written consent before any test
c: Passengers must also take a breath test
d: By driving, you have agreed to a chemical test if police lawfully ask
exp: Accepting a license means you agreed in advance to breath, blood or urine testing when an officer suspects impaired driving.
src: State driver manuals, implied consent section

q: An officer who suspects impaired driving asks you to take a breath test and you refuse. What usually happens?
a: Your license is suspended for refusing
b: Nothing, because refusing is your right
c: You get a written warning
d: You must take a driving test again later
exp: Refusal carries its own penalties under implied consent laws, and in most states that includes a license suspension.
src: State driver manuals, implied consent section

q: Which chemical tests can be used to measure alcohol or drugs in a driver?
a: Breath only
b: Breath, blood or urine
c: Blood only
d: Saliva and hair only
exp: Implied consent laws cover breath, blood and urine tests. Blood tests can also find drugs a breath test cannot.
src: State driver manuals, implied consent section

q: What is an ignition interlock?
a: A lock that stops the car from going over the speed limit
b: A device that disables your phone while driving
c: A seat belt switch that keeps the car in park
d: A breath tester that keeps the car from starting if it detects alcohol
exp: Courts often require an ignition interlock after an impaired driving offense. The engine will not start until the driver gives a clean breath sample.
src: NHTSA, Drunk Driving; state driver manuals

q: Which statement about impaired driving penalties is true?
a: Penalties grow with repeat offenses and higher BAC
b: A first offense only brings a warning
c: Penalties are the same for every offense
d: Only drivers under 21 can lose their license
exp: In every state, penalties climb with each offense and with a higher BAC.
src: State driver manuals, DUI penalties section

q: You must carry an opened bottle of wine home from a dinner. Where is the best place to put it?
a: In the cup holder
b: In the trunk
c: On the front passenger floor
d: In the glove box
exp: Open containers are banned in the passenger area in most states. The trunk keeps it out of reach of the driver and passengers.
src: 23 U.S.C. 154 (open container); state driver manuals

q: Your allergy medicine label says it may cause drowsiness. What should you do?
a: Drive, because it is a legal medicine
b: Drink coffee and drive
c: Avoid driving until you know how it affects you
d: Drive only on the highway
exp: Legal medicines can impair you, and driving impaired by any drug is illegal. Check the label and find out how it affects you first.
src: NHTSA, Drug Impaired Driving; state driver manuals

q: Which statement about marijuana and driving is true?
a: It slows reaction time and is illegal to drive impaired by, even where it is legal to buy
b: It is safe to drive on in states where it is legal
c: It only affects driving at night
d: It improves focus on long drives
exp: Marijuana slows reactions and hurts lane control. Driving impaired by it is illegal in every state.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/drug-impaired-driving

q: Why is mixing a small amount of alcohol with a cold medicine dangerous for a driver?
a: The medicine cancels out the alcohol
b: The two together can impair you more than either one alone
c: Cold medicine raises your legal BAC limit
d: It is only dangerous for drivers over 65
exp: Alcohol and many medicines boost each other's effects, so a small amount of each can cause serious impairment.
src: State driver manuals, drugs and alcohol section

q: You went to a party and your ride has been drinking. What is the best choice?
a: Ride along but make sure everyone wears a seat belt
b: Offer to keep the driver talking so they stay alert
c: Find another ride, such as a sober friend, a ride service or a parent
d: Ride with them if the trip is short
exp: Never ride with an impaired driver. A sober driver, a ride service or a call home keeps you out of that car.
src: NHTSA, Drunk Driving; state driver manuals

q: What are the three kinds of driver distraction?
a: Noise, light and heat
b: Early, late and sudden
c: Passenger, phone and radio
d: Visual, manual and cognitive
exp: Distractions take your eyes off the road (visual), your hands off the wheel (manual) or your mind off driving (cognitive).
src: CDC, Distracted Driving; state driver manuals

q: Why is texting while driving so dangerous?
a: It only affects your hearing
b: It takes your eyes, hands and mind off driving
c: It is only risky above 55 mph
d: It mainly drains the car battery
exp: Texting is a visual, manual and cognitive distraction at the same time.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/distracted-driving

q: Reading a text takes your eyes off the road for about five seconds. At 55 mph, how far do you travel in that time?
a: About one car length
b: About the length of a school bus
c: About the length of a football field
d: About a mile
exp: NHTSA compares five seconds at 55 mph to driving the length of a football field with your eyes closed.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/distracted-driving

q: Which statement about hands-free phone calls is true?
a: They are completely safe
b: They are safer than talking to a passenger
c: They are allowed for all teen drivers in every state
d: They still take your mind off driving
exp: A call is a cognitive distraction even when your hands are free, and a passenger, unlike a caller, can see the road.
src: NHTSA, Distracted Driving; state driver manuals

q: While you are driving, your sunglasses fall onto the floor. What should you do?
a: Leave them until you have parked
b: Reach down quickly to grab them
c: Ask the driver behind you to wait
d: Slow to 10 mph and reach for them
exp: Reaching for a dropped item is a visual and manual distraction that can pull you out of your lane. Wait until you park.
src: State driver manuals, distracted driving section

q: You are driving on a highway and keep yawning, and you cannot remember the last few miles. What should you do?
a: Open the window and keep driving
b: Turn up the radio
c: Pull off at a safe place and rest
d: Speed up to get home sooner
exp: These are warning signs of drowsy driving. The only real fix is rest, so stop at a safe place.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/drowsy-driving

q: When do drowsy driving crashes happen most often?
a: Between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m.
b: Around noon
c: Right after sunrise on weekends
d: Between midnight and 6 a.m. and in the late afternoon
exp: Drowsy crashes peak when the body clock dips: late night to early morning and late afternoon.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/drowsy-driving

q: What is a micro-sleep?
a: A brief sleep of a few seconds that can happen without warning
b: A planned 20 minute nap at a rest area
c: A feeling of being slightly tired
d: A type of sleep medicine
exp: A micro-sleep lasts about four or five seconds, long enough to cover more than 100 yards at highway speed with no one steering.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/drowsy-driving

q: Which of these is the best way to avoid drowsy driving on a long trip?
a: Drink an energy drink every hour
b: Get a full night of sleep and take regular breaks
c: Drive at night when roads are empty
d: Keep the car cold and the music loud
exp: Sleep is the only real protection. Caffeine helps only briefly and does not replace rest.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/drowsy-driving

q: A driver behind you is tailgating and flashing their lights. What should you do?
a: Brake hard to warn them
b: Speed up to get away
c: Make eye contact and gesture back
d: Move over when it is safe and let them pass
exp: Give an aggressive driver room and avoid any response that could start a conflict.
src: NHTSA, Aggressive Driving; state driver manuals

q: An angry driver is following you after a disagreement. Where should you go?
a: To a police station or a busy, well lit place, and call 911
b: Straight home
c: To a quiet side street to talk it out
d: Into an empty parking lot
exp: Do not lead an angry driver to your home or stop to argue. Go somewhere safe and public and call for help.
src: State driver manuals, road rage section

q: How should the lap part of a seat belt be worn?
a: Low and snug across the hips
b: Across the stomach
c: Loose so you can move
d: Above the belly button
exp: The lap belt belongs across the hips, not the stomach, where the bones can take the force of a crash.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/seat-belts

q: Where should the shoulder belt go?
a: Behind your back
b: Across the middle of the chest and away from the neck
c: Under your arm
d: Across your neck
exp: The shoulder belt crosses the chest and shoulder. Putting it behind your back or under your arm can cause serious injuries.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/seat-belts

q: Your car has airbags. Do you still need to wear a seat belt?
a: No, airbags replace seat belts
b: Only on highways
c: Yes, airbags are designed to work with seat belts
d: Only in the back seat
exp: Airbags add protection but do not replace belts. An unbelted person can be badly hurt by an airbag as it opens.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/seat-belts; https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/air-bags

q: About how far should your chest be from the airbag cover in the steering wheel?
a: At least 2 inches
b: Exactly 4 inches
c: No more than 6 inches
d: At least 10 inches
exp: NHTSA advises at least 10 inches between your breastbone and the airbag cover.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/air-bags

q: Where should a rear-facing child seat never be placed?
a: In the back seat
b: In front of an active airbag
c: Behind the driver
d: In the middle of the back seat
exp: A deploying front airbag can strike a rear-facing seat and seriously injure the baby.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/air-bags

q: Up to what age should children ride in the back seat?
a: Through age 4
b: Through age 8
c: Through age 12
d: Only while in a car seat
exp: NHTSA recommends that children 12 and under ride in the back seat.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/car-seats-and-booster-seats

q: A child has outgrown a forward-facing seat with a harness but the adult belt crosses her neck and stomach. What should she use?
a: The adult belt alone
b: A rear-facing seat
c: The front seat with the airbag on
d: A booster seat
exp: A booster raises the child so the adult belt fits correctly. Stay in it until the belt fits without it.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/car-seats-and-booster-seats

q: When does a child no longer need a booster seat?
a: When the lap belt lies on the upper thighs and the shoulder belt crosses the chest
b: On the child's 6th birthday
c: When the child can buckle the belt alone
d: When the child weighs as much as a small adult passenger
exp: Fit decides, not age alone. The lap belt must sit on the upper thighs and the shoulder belt on the chest and shoulder.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/car-seats-and-booster-seats

q: How long should a baby stay in a rear-facing seat?
a: Only until the first birthday
b: Only for the first three months
c: Until reaching the seat's top height or weight limit
d: Until the baby can sit up alone
exp: Keep children rear-facing as long as possible, up to the seat's limits.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/car-seats-and-booster-seats

q: It is a mild day and you need to run into a store for two minutes. Your toddler is asleep in the car. What should you do?
a: Leave the child with the windows cracked
b: Leave the engine running with the air on
c: Park in the shade and lock the doors
d: Take the child with you
exp: Never leave a child alone in a car for any length of time. A child heats up three to five times faster than an adult.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/campaign/heatstroke

q: Which habit helps prevent a child from being forgotten in a car?
a: Checking the back seat every time before you lock the car
b: Parking in the shade
c: Cracking the windows
d: Leaving the car unlocked
exp: More than half of child hot car deaths happen when a caregiver forgets the child. Look before you lock.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/campaign/heatstroke

q: You see a child alone in a locked, hot car. What should you do?
a: Wait 30 minutes for the parent
b: Call 911 right away
c: Leave a note on the windshield
d: Report it at the end of the day
exp: A child in a hot car can be in danger within minutes. NHTSA advises calling 911 immediately.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/campaign/heatstroke

q: A red light shaped like an oil can comes on while you are driving. What should you do?
a: Keep driving and check it next week
b: Turn on the heater
c: Speed up to reach home faster
d: Pull over safely and turn off the engine
exp: Red means a serious problem. Low oil pressure can quickly destroy the engine.
src: Owner's manual warning lights; State driver manuals, vehicle equipment and pre-drive checks

q: In general, what does a yellow or amber dashboard warning light mean?
a: Something needs attention soon
b: A system is simply turned on
c: The car must be stopped at once
d: Your high beams are on
exp: Yellow lights flag a problem to check soon. Red lights are more urgent, and green or blue lights are information.
src: Owner's manual warning lights; State driver manuals, vehicle equipment and pre-drive checks

q: A blue light shaped like a headlight is on in your dashboard. What does it mean?
a: The engine is overheating
b: Your high beams are on
c: A tire is low
d: The brakes have failed
exp: The blue headlight symbol shows that the high beams are on.
src: Owner's manual warning lights; State driver manuals, vehicle equipment and pre-drive checks

q: Where do you find the correct air pressure for your car's tires?
a: On the tire's sidewall
b: At the top of the windshield
c: On the sticker inside the driver's door frame or in the owner's manual
d: On the registration card
exp: The number on the sidewall is the tire's maximum, not the right pressure for your car.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/equipment/tires

q: When is the best time to check tire pressure?
a: When the tires are cold
b: Right after a long highway drive
c: Only in summer
d: Only when a tire looks flat
exp: Driving warms the tires and raises the reading, so check before driving.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/equipment/tires

q: Why are tires with worn tread dangerous?
a: They make the car use less fuel
b: They are more likely to skid and hydroplane on wet roads
c: They make steering too heavy
d: They cause the horn to fail
exp: Tread grooves push water out from under the tire. Worn tread loses that grip.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/equipment/tires

q: Your brake pedal feels soft and sinks lower than usual. What does that most likely mean?
a: The brakes are working normally
b: The tires need air
c: The brakes need a mechanic's attention soon
d: The parking brake is on
exp: A soft or sinking pedal is a sign of a brake problem that should be fixed right away.
src: State driver manuals, vehicle equipment and pre-drive checks

q: A turn signal starts blinking much faster than usual. What is the most likely cause?
a: The battery is fully charged
b: The car is low on fuel
c: The hazard lights are broken
d: A signal bulb has burned out
exp: On many cars, a fast blinking signal means one of the signal bulbs is out.
src: State driver manuals, vehicle equipment and pre-drive checks

q: How should you set your side mirrors?
a: So you see mostly your own car
b: So you barely see the side of your own car at the inner edge
c: Pointed at the road surface
d: Folded in while driving
exp: This setting reduces the blind spot. You must still turn your head before changing lanes.
src: State driver manuals, vehicle equipment and pre-drive checks

q: Even with well set mirrors, what must you do before changing lanes?
a: Honk your horn
b: Flash your headlights
c: Turn your head and check your blind spot
d: Brake firmly
exp: Every car has blind spots that no mirror shows. A quick look over your shoulder covers them.
src: State driver manuals, vehicle equipment and pre-drive checks

q: Where should the middle of the head restraint be?
a: At the base of your neck
b: Below your shoulders
c: Removed for comfort
d: About level with the tops of your ears
exp: A head restraint set too low cannot stop your head snapping back in a rear end crash.
src: IIHS head restraint guidance; State driver manuals, vehicle equipment and pre-drive checks

q: Why should you keep the floor near the pedals clear?
a: A loose object can roll under a pedal and keep you from braking
b: It improves fuel economy
c: It keeps the car cooler
d: It is needed for the dashboard lights to work
exp: A bottle or bag under the brake pedal can stop it from moving when you need it most.
src: State driver manuals, vehicle equipment and pre-drive checks

q: Why should you wear a seat belt even on a short, slow trip near home?
a: Seat belts work only at low speed
b: A belt is needed only to pass the road test
c: Most crashes happen close to home at everyday speeds
d: Short trips are covered by airbags alone
exp: Every trip carries crash risk, and most crashes are not on highways.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/seat-belts

q: What is one of the main ways a seat belt saves lives?
a: It makes the airbag open faster
b: It lowers your speed before a crash
c: It keeps the car from skidding
d: It keeps you from being thrown out of the car
exp: Being thrown from a vehicle is almost always deadly. A belt keeps you inside and in your seat.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/seat-belts

q: A pregnant passenger asks how to wear her seat belt. What is correct?
a: Lap belt below the belly across the hips, shoulder belt across the chest
b: No belt, only the airbag
c: Lap belt across the middle of the belly
d: Shoulder belt behind the back
exp: Doctors recommend wearing a belt through pregnancy, with the lap belt below the belly.
src: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/seat-belts

q: Which documents should you have with you when you drive?
a: Your birth certificate and passport
b: Your license, the vehicle registration and proof of insurance
c: Only your license
d: Your school ID and the car's title
exp: An officer can ask for all three at any traffic stop.
src: State driver manuals, licensing and insurance section

q: What does liability insurance pay for?
a: Repairs to your own car after any crash
b: Your own medical bills only
c: Routine maintenance
d: Injuries and damage you cause to other people
exp: Liability coverage protects others you harm. Repairing your own car takes collision coverage.
src: State driver manuals, insurance section

q: What does a vehicle registration prove?
a: That the car is registered with the state
b: That the driver is licensed
c: That the car is insured
d: That the car passed a driving test
exp: Registration shows the vehicle is on record with the state. Your license and insurance card are separate documents.
src: State driver manuals, registration section

q: A week before your knowledge test, you take a mock exam and miss 9 questions. What is the best use of your next study session?
a: Reread the sections behind the questions you missed
b: Reread the chapters you already know well
c: Take the same mock exam again right away
d: Stop studying so you do not get confused
exp: Studying your misses raises your score; rereading what you already know does not.
src: Permit Path study method; state manuals advise studying the full manual before testing (PennDOT Driver's Manual, Testing (pa.gov/agencies/dmv))

q: Where should you get the numbers for your numbers sheet, such as speed limits and BAC limits?
a: From a friend who already has a license
b: From any website about driving
c: From your state's rules in Chapter 1 and the state boxes
d: From memory of what other drivers do
exp: Many of these numbers differ by state, so take them from your state's official rules.
src: State driver manuals; PennDOT Driver's Manual, Testing (pa.gov/agencies/dmv)

q: What is usually the better choice the night before your knowledge test?
a: Study late into the night to cover every chapter
b: Do a light review, pack your documents and get a full night's sleep
c: Skip dinner so you feel alert
d: Learn new topics you have not studied yet
exp: A rested brain reads questions more carefully, and careful reading wins points.
src: Permit Path study method

q: A test question asks, "Which of these is NOT a reason to slow down?" What should you do first?
a: Pick the first answer that is a reason to slow down
b: Skip it, since trick questions are not scored
c: Answer from what most drivers do
d: Read the whole question and notice the word NOT before you look at the answers
exp: Small words like NOT and EXCEPT flip the meaning. Read the whole question before choosing.
src: Permit Path test tactics

q: You are not sure of an answer. What is a smart way to improve your odds?
a: Rule out answers you know are wrong, then choose among the rest
b: Always pick the longest answer
c: Always pick answer C
d: Pick the answer that gets you through the hazard fastest
exp: Crossing off clearly wrong choices turns a four-way guess into a smaller choice.
src: Permit Path test tactics

q: When two answers on the knowledge test both sound reasonable, which one should you pick?
a: The one you have seen other drivers do most often
b: The one that matches the rule in the official manual
c: The one that saves the most time
d: The one that assumes other drivers will follow the law
exp: Each question is written to have one answer based on the official manual.
src: State driver manuals; PennDOT Driver's Manual, Testing (pa.gov/agencies/dmv)

q: When should you change an answer you already chose on the knowledge test?
a: Whenever you feel nervous about it
b: Never, under any circumstances
c: Only when you find a real reason, such as a word you misread
d: Whenever the next question seems easier
exp: Changes made out of nerves are more often wrong. Change only when you find a real error.
src: Permit Path test tactics

q: Your knowledge test screen stops before you reach the last question. What does that usually mean?
a: The computer has crashed and you must restart
b: You were caught cheating
c: You ran out of time on every question
d: Your state may end the test early once you pass or once you cannot pass; read the result
exp: Some states stop the test as soon as the result is certain.
src: Permit Path test tactics; state testing pages

q: What happens in most states if you use your phone or notes during the knowledge test?
a: Nothing, as long as you are quiet
b: You may only look up sign pictures
c: Your test can be ended
d: You lose one point
exp: Phones, notes and talking are not allowed once the test starts, and using them can end the test.
src: State testing rules; PennDOT Driver's Manual, Testing (pa.gov/agencies/dmv)

q: Which item should you bring for the road test in nearly every state?
a: A photo of your car
b: Your learner permit and the car's current registration and proof of insurance
c: A letter from your school
d: Your own score sheet
exp: Testing offices check your permit and the car's papers. Missing or expired papers usually mean no test.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Testing (pa.gov/agencies/dmv); California DMV, Behind the Wheel Drive Test Preparation (FFDL 22); New York DMV, Prepare for your road test (dmv.ny.gov)

q: You need glasses to pass the vision test. What is the likely result?
a: Your license may say you must wear them when you drive
b: You cannot get a license
c: You only need them at night
d: You must take the road test twice
exp: If you pass the vision test with glasses or contacts, your license usually requires you to drive with them.
src: New York DMV, Prepare for your road test (dmv.ny.gov); state driver manuals

q: At the start of the road test, the examiner finds that one of your brake lights does not work. What usually happens?
a: The examiner fixes it for you
b: You take the test and lose a few points
c: The test is not given and you must reschedule
d: You may take the test in daylight only
exp: Most states will not test in a car that is not safe and legal.
src: California DMV, Behind the Wheel Drive Test Preparation (FFDL 22); PennDOT Driver's Manual, Testing (pa.gov/agencies/dmv)

q: Which of these is commonly checked during the pre-test vehicle check?
a: The radio presets
b: The car's paint color
c: The air freshener
d: Lights, horn, brakes, mirrors, tires and seat belts
exp: Examiners check the parts that make the car safe and legal before the drive.
src: California DMV, Behind the Wheel Drive Test Preparation (FFDL 22); PennDOT Driver's Manual, Testing (pa.gov/agencies/dmv)

q: Before you drive away, the examiner asks you to show the defroster and the emergency flashers. What is the examiner checking?
a: That you can find and use the car's controls
b: That the car is new
c: That you have read the owner's manual cover to cover
d: That your parent taught you
exp: Many road tests begin with a controls check: lights, wipers, defroster, flashers, horn and parking brake.
src: PennDOT Driver's Manual, Testing (pa.gov/agencies/dmv); California DMV, Behind the Wheel Drive Test Preparation (FFDL 22)

q: A friend wants to ride along in the back seat during your road test for moral support. What is the general rule?
a: Any passenger may ride along if they stay quiet
b: Friends usually cannot ride along; only people your state allows, often just you and the examiner
c: A friend may ride along if they have a license
d: Passengers are required for the test
exp: States limit who may be in the car during the test, and many allow only the applicant and the examiner.
src: Minnesota DPS road test guidance; New York DMV, Prepare for your road test (dmv.ny.gov)

q: Before you pull away from the curb, what is the correct order?
a: Pull out, then signal
b: Check the mirror, pull out, then signal
c: Signal, check mirrors, turn your head to check your blind spot, then pull out when safe
d: Honk, then pull out
exp: Signal, mirror and a head check before moving is what examiners look for when you leave the curb.
src: New York DMV, Road Test Results scoring categories (dmv.ny.gov); California DMV, Driving Test Criteria (DL 955)

q: You stop at a stop sign, but your wheels are still slowly rolling. On a road test, this is called:
a: A rolling stop, and it is a common automatic fail
b: A smooth stop, and it earns points
c: A legal stop if no one is coming
d: A safe stop if you are below 5 mph
exp: A stop means the wheels are not moving. Rolling through a stop sign is a serious error on road tests.
src: California DMV, Driving Test Criteria (DL 955); PennDOT Driver's Manual, Testing (pa.gov/agencies/dmv)

q: You stop behind another car at a red light. How much space should you leave?
a: Touch its bumper to save space
